name: Introduction to AI and the Future Workforce
objectives: Given a list of work tasks, explain what AI is, name ways it is changing civilian jobs and identify which skills it does not replace, getting at least 4 of 5 right

chapters.name: Chapter 1: AI basics for the mission ahead

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What AI is and how it is changing work
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain in your own words what AI is and name two ways it is changing civilian jobs.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of work tasks, you will explain what AI is, name ways it is changing civilian jobs and identify which skills it does not replace, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
AI, or artificial intelligence, means computer programs that do tasks that usually need a person, such as writing, summarizing, sorting information or spotting patterns. An AI assistant is one you chat with in everyday words. Well-known free ones include ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini.
In civilian work, AI is now used to draft emails and reports, summarize long documents, plan schedules and routes, answer customer questions, and find problems in data. In logistics it helps forecast supplies; in maintenance it helps spot parts likely to fail; in offices it writes first drafts.
AI does not replace judgment, leadership or responsibility. Those are skills you built in uniform. Employers want people who can use AI as a tool and still make the call, check the work and lead the team.
Words to know:
- AI: short for artificial intelligence: computer programs that do tasks that usually need a person.
- AI assistant: an AI program you chat with by typing or talking.
Try it now: Write down two tasks from your military job and two tasks from a civilian job you want. Next to each, write one way AI could help with it.
You can now explain what AI is, name ways it is changing work, and say which skills AI does not replace.

check.q: Which task is AI best at in a civilian job?
options: Drafting a first version of a report
Taking responsibility for the final decision
Earning trust with a team
Leading people in a crisis
check.why: AI can draft and sort information, but judgment, trust and leadership stay with people.

check.q: A coworker says AI will make your leadership skills useless. What do you say?
options: Agree and stop listing leadership
Say AI does not replace judgment, leadership or responsibility
Say AI is only used in the military
Say AI is always right, so people only type
check.why: AI changes tasks, but people still lead, decide and are responsible.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Opening an assistant and giving a clear order
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Open a free AI assistant and write a prompt with a task, conditions and a standard.
This lesson builds toward: Using a phone or computer, you will open a free AI assistant and write a prompt with a task, conditions and a standard, so the first answer is useful.
On a phone, install the official app from the app store (OpenAI for ChatGPT, Microsoft for Copilot, Google for Gemini). On a computer, type chatgpt.com, copilot.microsoft.com or gemini.google.com in the browser.
What you type is called a prompt. You already know how to give a clear order. Use the same idea: the task (what you need), the conditions (your situation), and the standard (what a good answer looks like: length, format, tone).
Example: "Task: list civilian jobs that use vehicle maintenance skills. Conditions: I was an Army light-wheel vehicle mechanic for 6 years. Standard: 5 job titles, one line each, plain words."
Step by step:
- Open the official app or website.
- Write the task: what you need.
- Add the conditions: your situation, without private details.
- Add the standard: length, format and tone.
- Send it and read the answer.
Words to know:
- Prompt: what you type or say to an AI assistant to ask for something.
- Format: the shape of the answer, such as a list, a table or a short paragraph.
Try it now: Open a free AI assistant. Write a prompt with task, conditions and standard asking for five civilian job titles that use the skills from your military job. Read the answer.
You can now open a free AI assistant and write a prompt with a task, conditions and a standard.

check.q: In a clear-order prompt, what is the task?
options: Your private details
How long the answer should be
What you want the AI to do
The name of the AI tool
check.why: The task is the job you give the AI; conditions and standard come after.

check.q: You want civilian job ideas from an AI assistant. Which prompt do you send?
options: "Jobs?"
"Tell me everything about work."
"Write my whole life story."
"Task: list civilian jobs. Conditions: 4 years as a supply specialist. Standard: 5 titles, one line each."
check.why: A prompt with a task, conditions and a standard gets a useful first answer.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Keeping private and sensitive information out
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check a prompt for private or sensitive information and remove it before you send it.
This lesson builds toward: Before you send any prompt, you will check it for private and sensitive information and remove it or replace it with a placeholder, sharing no private numbers and no classified, controlled or mission details.
Public AI assistants may store what you type. Never type your Social Security number, the numbers on your DD-214, VA file or claim numbers, bank or card numbers, passwords, or medical details you would not want shared.
The same discipline you used for operational security (OPSEC) applies. Do not type classified or controlled information, unit locations, mission details, or anything you were told not to share. Describe your work in general terms: "supervised a 12-person maintenance team" is fine; unit names and missions are not needed.
If you need a number in a document, write a placeholder like "[my number]" and fill it in yourself later, offline.
Step by step:
- Read your prompt before you send it.
- Remove personal numbers, account details and passwords.
- Remove classified, controlled or mission-specific details.
- Use a placeholder like "[my number]" where needed.
Words to know:
- OPSEC: operational security: protecting information an adversary could use.
- Placeholder: a stand-in like "[my number]" that you replace later yourself.
- DD-214: the document that records your service and discharge.
Try it now: Write a prompt describing your last military job in a way you could share with any employer. Read it line by line and remove anything private or sensitive before sending.
You can now check a prompt for private and sensitive information and remove it before you send it.

check.q: You are drafting a cover letter with AI and need your phone number in it. What do you do?
options: Type the real number so the letter is finished
Write "[my phone]" and add the real number yourself later
Type your Social Security number instead
Ask the AI to guess a number
check.why: A placeholder gets you the help without putting a private number into the AI.

check.q: Which detail is safe to put in a public AI prompt?
options: "Trained 8 new team members on safety checks"
Your unit's deployment dates and location
Details from a classified briefing
Your VA file number
check.why: General duties with numbers are fine; mission details and private numbers stay out.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Translating your service into civilian work

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Finding the civilian jobs that match your service
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Look up your military job in the O*NET Military Crosswalk and list matching civilian jobs.
This lesson builds toward: Given your military job code or title, you will look up your military job in the O*NET Military Crosswalk and list matching civilian jobs, with at least three civilian job titles and two tasks for each.
The U.S. Department of Labor's O*NET OnLine has a Military Crosswalk Search. You choose your branch (Army or Marine Corps MOS, Navy or Coast Guard rating, Air Force AFSC, Space Force SFSC), type your code or job title, and it shows civilian occupations that match.
Each civilian occupation on O*NET lists its tasks, tools and skills. That is the language employers use. You can then ask an AI assistant to explain those jobs in plain words, but the list itself comes from the official source.
CareerOneStop, also sponsored by the Department of Labor, has a Veterans Job Matcher that does a similar match. Try both and compare.
Step by step:
- Go to onetonline.org and open the Military Crosswalk Search.
- Choose your branch.
- Type your code (for example 88M or a Navy rating) or job title.
- Open two or three matching civilian occupations and read their tasks.
- Write down the job titles that interest you.
Words to know:
- MOS / rating / AFSC: the code for your military job in the Army and Marines, Navy and Coast Guard, and Air Force.
- Crosswalk: a tool that matches a military job to civilian jobs.
- O*NET: the Department of Labor's database of civilian jobs and the skills they need.
Official sources:
- O*NET OnLine: Military Crosswalk Search
- U.S. Department of Labor VETS: Find a job
Try it now: Look up your MOS, rating or AFSC in the O*NET Military Crosswalk. Write down three civilian job titles it suggests and two tasks from each.
You can now use the O*NET Military Crosswalk to find civilian jobs that match your military job.

check.q: What do you type into the O*NET Military Crosswalk to find matching jobs?
options: Your Social Security number
Your home address
Your favorite civilian company
Your military job code or title
check.why: The crosswalk searches by military job code or title and shows matching civilian occupations.

check.q: The crosswalk shows several civilian jobs for your code. What do you do next?
options: Pick the first one without reading
Ignore the list and ask a friend
Write down three job titles and two tasks for each
Close it and guess a job title
check.why: Writing down titles and their tasks gives you civilian words to use in your résumé.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Rewriting a military duty in civilian words
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to rewrite one military duty as a civilian résumé bullet with a result.
This lesson builds toward: Given one duty from your service, you will use an AI assistant to rewrite the duty as civilian résumé bullets with a size and a result, with no military slang and every claim true.
Civilian hiring managers may not know what a platoon sergeant, a PMCS or a CONEX is. Your job is to say the same thing in their words: what you did, how big it was, and what result it got.
Give the AI your duty in plain terms and the civilian job you are aiming for. Example prompt: "Rewrite this for a warehouse supervisor résumé: I was responsible for a supply room, 300 line items, issued gear to 120 soldiers, zero losses on 2 inventories. Give me 3 bullets that start with a strong verb and include numbers."
Then improve it with follow-ups: "Remove military slang." "Use the words from this job posting." "Make it shorter." The first answer is a draft; you are the editor.
Step by step:
- Write the duty in plain words: what, how big, what result.
- Name the civilian job you are aiming for.
- Ask for 3 bullets with strong verbs and numbers.
- Ask for one change, like "remove military slang".
- Read it and make sure every word is true.
Words to know:
- Résumé bullet: one short line on a résumé that shows something you did and its result.
- Acronym: a word made from first letters, like PMCS; civilians often do not know military ones.
Try it now: Pick one duty from your service. Ask an AI assistant to rewrite it as three civilian résumé bullets for one job title from Lesson 4. Ask it to remove military slang.
You can now rewrite a military duty as clear, civilian résumé bullets with numbers and results.

check.q: Which résumé bullet is written for a civilian employer?
options: "Led a 10-person team that cut equipment repair time by 20%"
"Served as NCOIC of the motor pool IAW SOP"
"Did various duties as assigned"
"Was in charge of stuff"
check.why: It uses plain words and shows what you did, how big it was and the result.

check.q: The AI's bullet still says "CONUS" and "PCS". What do you ask next?
options: "Add more acronyms."
"Make it longer."
"Remove military slang and use plain civilian words."
"Write it as a poem."
check.why: A follow-up asking to remove slang turns the draft into words a civilian reader understands.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Checking the answer and planning your next skill
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check an AI answer against official sources and choose one skill to build next.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI answer about jobs, pay or programs, you will check the answer against official sources and choose one skill and one program for your next step, before you use it.
AI can make things up: a job title that does not fit, a certification that does not exist, or a wrong pay figure. This is called a hallucination. Check job titles against O*NET, and check pay and job outlook in the Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook (bls.gov/ooh).
Make sure your bullets are true. Never let AI inflate your rank, numbers or awards. An employer may check, and trust is hard to win back.
Then plan one skill to build. Free official help includes the VA's Personalized Career Planning and Guidance program (free career counseling for eligible veterans and service members) and the Department of Labor's Transition Assistance Program. For high-tech training, the VA's VET TEC 2.0 program pays for certain non-degree tech courses for eligible veterans. Check current eligibility on va.gov.
Step by step:
- Check every job title against O*NET.
- Check pay and outlook in the Occupational Outlook Handbook.
- Make sure every number and claim in your bullets is true.
- Pick one skill to build and one official program that can help.
Words to know:
- Hallucination: when an AI writes something that sounds true but is made up.
- Occupational Outlook Handbook: a free Bureau of Labor Statistics guide to pay, job growth and how to enter each job.
Official sources:
- Bureau of Labor Statistics: Occupational Outlook Handbook
- VA: Personalized Career Planning and Guidance
- VA: VET TEC 2.0
- U.S. Department of Labor: Transition Assistance Program
Try it now: Final task: take your three bullets from Lesson 5. Check the job titles in the O*NET Military Crosswalk, ask the AI for one improvement, remove any private or sensitive details, and save the final bullets.
You can now check AI career answers against official sources and pick one skill and one program for your next step.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear prompt The prompt is vague, for example "fix my résumé". The prompt has a task, conditions and a standard. It also names the civilian job title, and the first answer is close to ready. Civilian words The bullets still use military slang or have no result. Three bullets in plain civilian words, each with what you did and a size or result. The learner asked for one improvement and can say what it fixed. Job titles checked Job titles were copied from the AI without checking. The job titles were checked in the O*NET Military Crosswalk. The learner also checked pay or outlook in the Occupational Outlook Handbook. Private and sensitive details out The prompt or bullets have a private number or a mission detail. No private numbers and no classified, controlled or mission details. Used placeholders and can explain why each removed detail had to go. Every claim true A bullet has a claim, number or award that is not true. Every claim and number in the bullets is true. The learner named one skill and one program for the next step. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: An AI answer that is always correct
A new AI tool for veterans
A way to make prompts shorter
Something an AI writes that sounds true but is made up
check.why: AI can make things up and still sound sure, so you check facts against official sources.

check.q: An AI tells you the average pay for a civilian job. What do you do before using it?
options: Put it on your résumé
Check it in the Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook
Ask the AI if it is sure
Share it with friends as fact
check.why: Pay figures come from official sources like the Occupational Outlook Handbook, not the AI.
